justification: Re-check focused on the two round-1 findings and a fresh full read; the rest of the article is unchanged in substance from round 1's 8.8 pass. (1) Near-duplicate opening example, now resolved. The article's opening now uses amount 12 (coins {1,4,5}) instead of 8: greedy picks 5+5+1+1=4 coins, brute force finds the true minimum is 3 (4+4+4), verified independently by re-running the exact MinCoins(12, [1,4,5]) recursion (best=3, calls=180 -- matches the article's 'min coins for 12: 3' / 'recursive calls: 180' exactly, digit for digit). This no longer collides with greedy-algorithms.md, which still asks its own 'prove it' exercise about amount 8 on the same coin set (greedy 5+1+1+1=4 vs. optimal 4+4=2) -- different amount, different optimal count, different pedagogical role (a reader-solved exercise there vs. the motivating worked example here), so a reviewer reading both pages back-to-back no longer sees the same instance solved twice. Figure 1 was correctly redrawn for amount 12: I traced the SVG's branch structure against the actual code (coins iterated in order [1,4,5], so 12 branches to 11/8/7, 11 branches to 10/7/6, 8 branches to 7/4/3) and it matches both the drawing and the caption's claim that remaining amount 7 is reached three times, via a 5 from 12, a 4 from 11, and a 1 from 8. The prose right after ('Four coins, but three 4s also add up to 12', 'confirming the 4-plus-4-plus-4 guess and beating greedy's four') reads as native to amount 12, not a patched find-and-replace -- no stray reference to 8, 2 coins, or the old figure anywhere in the file. 'How bad it gets' (amounts 10/20/30/40) and every section after tabulation (amount 23, the 0..200 agreement check) were already independent of the opening instance and needed no rederivation; none shows any inconsistency with the new amount 12. (2) The CLRS chapter-14 citation is unchanged (front matter + two inline citations, all chapter 14) and per this round's brief is confirmed correct and out of scope; worth noting the sibling greedy-algorithms.md has also since settled on chapter 14 for Dynamic Programming in its own source list, so the two articles that previously disagreed now agree. (3) The knapsack-cost gap from round 1 is NOT fixed: the closing paragraph still states knapsack's recurrence (best[i,w] = skip vs. take) and says it reuses 'the identical row-by-row fill and the identical space-optimization argument' but never states the cost itself (O(items x capacity) time, reducible to O(capacity) space) the way every other named technique on the page does -- see issues[]. Nothing else regressed: no filler, no NEEDS_MARKUS, no ad code, front matter still accurate and non-clickbait, exercises still varied in form and free of giveaways, and the article still delivers the 'one problem through every stage' structural angle that differentiates it from GeeksforGeeks (which solves a different coin-change variant) and Wikipedia's abstract LCS/edit-distance pages. Score moves up from 8.8 because two of the three round-1 findings are now closed (the duplicate resolved, the citation confirmed non-issue) and only the pre-existing low-severity knapsack-cost gap remains open.
